meta.title: Indoor Climbing — Technique Guide & Drill Bank
meta.subtitle: A complete reference for indoor climbers

tagLegend.core: learn first. Pays off immediately, little injury risk.
tagLegend.later: useful, once the core set is solid.
tagLegend.advanced: worth knowing by name; relevant at higher grades or in competition.
tagLegend.caution: meaningful injury risk, especially for fingers and elbows. Introduce late, never while something already hurts.

nonstandardNote: marks a name that is not standardised across gyms. The move is real; the label may differ.

sections.title: Principles
sections.body:
Climbing rewards technique long before it rewards strength. A beginner who moves well on V2 will pass a stronger beginner who thrashes on V4 within a season. Everything in this guide follows from a few ideas:

- **Quality of movement beats grade.** A clean V2 builds more than a scrappy V4. The grade measures the problem, not the climber.
- **Train one grade below your limit.** Hard enough to be interesting, easy enough that technique doesn't collapse. Limit-level attempts teach you to fight; sub-limit climbing teaches you to move.
- **Easy problems are the medium for drills,** not the destination. Make them hard with constraints, not with more grades.
- **Power arrives before tissue is ready for it.** Muscle adapts in weeks; tendons, pulleys and connective tissue take months to years. Almost every beginner injury lives in that gap.
- **Volume beats intensity early on.** More time on the wall moving well, less time hanging off two-finger edges.
- **2–4 sessions per week, non-consecutive.** Rest is when adaptation actually happens.
- **Skip for a while:** hangboarding, campus board, and dyno-heavy sessions. These add load without teaching movement, and they are where beginners get hurt.

sections.title: Staying Uninjured
sections.body:
Climbing injuries are overwhelmingly overuse injuries, not accidents. The common ones, roughly in order of frequency:

- **Finger pulleys (A2)** — pain at the base of a finger, usually from crimping hard too soon. The classic beginner injury.
- **Medial elbow (golfer's elbow)** — pain on the inside of the elbow, from overgripping, crimping and bent-arm climbing.
- **Lateral elbow (climber's elbow / tennis elbow)** — pain on the outside, often from open-hand and sloper work, or from too much campusing.
- **Shoulders** — usually from repeated lock-offs, gastons, and uncontrolled dynos without any pushing work to balance them.
- **Knees** — almost always drop knees and heel hooks applied violently or cold.

**What actually prevents them**

- **Warm up properly.** 15 minutes: general movement, then wrists, forearms, elbows and shoulders, then progressively harder climbing. Never start on a project.
- **Climb with straight arms.** Bent-arm hanging is the single biggest avoidable load on the elbows.
- **Relax the grip.** Overgripping wastes energy and drives elbow and finger problems.
- **Delay full crimping.** Use open hand and half crimp for the first year or more.
- **Train antagonists 2–3×/week:** push-ups, rows, shoulder external rotation, wrist extensors and flexors. Climbers become pull-dominant fast and the joints pay for it.
- **Progress load slowly.** Adding grades, sessions and volume all at once is how a good month becomes a bad quarter.

**Reading pain**

- Dull, warm, symmetrical soreness that fades in a day: normal training response.
- Sharp, localised, or one-sided pain, or pain that gets worse during a session: stop climbing on it that day.
- A pop, click, or sudden sharp pain in a finger: stop immediately.
- Pain that persists between sessions, or returns stronger each time, needs assessment rather than more rest and hope.

> This guide is general information, not medical advice. Any pain that is sharp, persistent, or getting worse is worth seeing a physiotherapist who works with climbers — early assessment is far cheaper than a six-month layoff.

sections.title: Footwork
sections.body:
**Precision.** Look at the foothold, choose the exact spot, place the toe there, then look away. Don't adjust. Don't slide. Most beginners place a foot, shuffle it twice, and lose body tension the whole time.

**Use the toe, not the arch.** Stand on the front point of the shoe. Inside edge (big-toe side) and outside edge (little-toe side) are your two main tools. Standing on the arch means you cannot pivot.

**Drop the heel.** Once the toe is placed, lower the heel. This tensions the calf and locks the shoe onto the hold. Heels-up climbing is why feet pop.

**Pivot, don't reposition.** With the toe fixed, the whole body can rotate around that point. Beginners re-place the foot when they could have simply turned the hip.

sections.title: Body Position
sections.body:
**Straight arms.** Hang from your skeleton, not your biceps. Bent arms burn forearms and load the elbow — the exact thing you're protecting. Bend only in the instant you pull for the next hold, then go straight again.

**Hips to the wall.** Weight sits over the feet instead of pulling out from the hands. Sagging hips means your arms are holding you on.

**Frontal vs. side-on.** Frontal (square to the wall, both inside edges) is stable but short-reaching. Side-on / twist-lock (one outside edge, hip turned into the wall) reaches much further and costs the arms far less. Switching between the two on demand is most of intermediate climbing.

**Backstep.** Outside edge of the foot on the hold, hip turned in. Turns a long reach into a short one. If you're straining to reach something, the answer is usually a backstep you didn't see.

**Flagging.** When a foot has nothing to stand on, extend that leg as a counterweight instead of letting it dangle. Same-side flag: leg extends out to its own side. Inside flag: leg crosses in front. Back flag: leg crosses behind — the most useful of the three.

**Drop knee.** From a backstep, rotate the knee downward to press into the foothold. Very powerful, and hard on the knee joint — use sparingly at this stage.

sections.title: Movement
sections.body:
- **Push with the legs; pull with the arms only to stay in balance.** Test: on an easy problem, move upward using legs while hands only touch lightly. You'll get further than you expect.
- **Move the centre of gravity first, then reach.** Shift weight over the new foot, then release the hand. Reaching first is what yanks people off the wall.
- **Deadpoint.** At the top of an upward move there is a weightless instant — that's when the hand should land. Not before, not after. Cheaper than a static lock-off and much kinder to the elbow.
- **Relax the grip.** Overgripping is wasted energy and a major elbow contributor.
- **Breathe.** Held breath means a tense body. Exhale on hard moves.

sections.title: Route Reading
sections.body:
Before touching the wall, identify: the hand sequence, which foot goes where, and where you can rest. Then climb it exactly as planned.

If it fails, ask **why the plan was wrong** rather than just trying harder. That habit separates the climbers who plateau from the ones who don't.

---

sections.title: Session Structure
sections.body:
| Block | Time | What |
|---|---|---|
| Warm-up | 15 min | Easy movement, then V0–V1. Wrists, forearms, elbows, shoulders. |
| Technique | 20–30 min | One drill from §13, on easy problems. Do this fresh, not tired. |
| Main climbing | 40–50 min | One grade below your limit. Quality of movement over completion. |
| Projecting | 15 min | A few attempts at your limit, only when fresh and pain-free. |
| Cool-down | 10 min | Easy downclimbing, light stretching, antagonist work. |

**Antagonist work** (2–3×/week, 10 minutes): push-ups, rows, shoulder external rotation, wrist extensors and flexors. Climbers become pull-dominant fast and the joints pay for it.

sections.title: Tracking Progress
sections.body:
Film one problem per session. Two things to look for:

1. How much time your arms spend bent.
2. How many times each foot moves after it's been placed.

Both numbers should trend down over weeks. That's technique improving, measurably.

**When to move up a grade.** The honest test for "this grade is boring": film yourself climbing it with one-touch and silent feet. If it's genuinely clean — no readjustments, no noise, no bent-arm hanging — move up. Most people find out it isn't.

**Session log — worth writing down**

- Which drill you used.
- Hardest problem climbed cleanly (not just completed).
- Any niggles: better / same / worse than last session.
- One technical thing that felt different.

techniqueCategories.title: Centre-of-Gravity Techniques
techniqueCategories.intro: These all do the same job: move body mass over the feet so the arms stop holding you on. For most climbers this is the highest-value category to work on.

techniqueCategories.title: Foot Techniques
techniqueCategories.intro: Everything here is about turning a foothold into something that can bear weight or pull you into the wall. Feet are where a beginner has the most unclaimed progress.

techniqueCategories.title: Hand & Grip Techniques
techniqueCategories.intro: Grip choice is where most finger and elbow injuries are made. Everything below is real technique, but the order you learn them in matters — the strongest grips are also the most stressful.

techniqueCategories.title: Positions & Hold Orientations
techniqueCategories.intro: The same hold can be four different holds depending on where your body is. This category is really about reading direction of pull.

techniqueCategories.title: Movement Techniques
techniqueCategories.intro: How you get from one position to the next. Most of these are cheap to learn and immediately useful.

techniqueCategories.title: Dynamic Techniques
techniqueCategories.intro: Powerful and fun, and the highest-impact category for tendons and joints. Ability here usually arrives before the tissue is ready for it, so restraint is the skill to build.

techniques.name: Back step
techniques.what: One foot on its outside edge with the hip turned into the wall, so your body goes side-on instead of square.
techniques.how: Place the little-toe edge on the hold, turn that hip toward the wall, let the opposite shoulder drop back. Your reaching arm now comes from a turned torso, not a stretch.
techniques.best: Long reaches, steep walls, and saving your arms. Learn this before anything else on this list.

techniques.name: Drop knee
techniques.what: A backstep taken further — the knee rotates downward and you actively press outward through the foot.
techniques.how: From a backstep with feet reasonably wide, rotate the knee down and in, pressing the foot into the hold. The pressure locks you in and pulls your hips to the wall.
techniques.best: Steep terrain and long reaches. Very hard on the knee joint (meniscus), so use sparingly and never with a violent rotation.

techniques.name: Outside flag
techniques.what: The free leg extends out to the same side it belongs to, acting as a counterweight.
techniques.how: Standing on one foot, swing the other leg out to its own side and press the toe lightly against the wall. Adjust how far out until the swing stops.
techniques.best: Stopping barn-doors when the free foot has nothing to stand on. The simplest flag — start here.

techniques.name: Back flag
techniques.what: The free leg crosses behind the standing leg and presses the wall.
techniques.how: Standing on the left foot, sweep the right leg behind the left and smear the toe on the wall to the left. Your hips turn side-on automatically.
techniques.best: The most useful flag in the gym. Fixes rotation on side-pulls and lets you reach far with one arm.

techniques.name: Inside flag
techniques.what: The free leg crosses in front of the standing leg.
techniques.how: Standing on one foot, bring the other leg across the front and press the toe on the wall or a foothold on the far side.
techniques.best: Tight, balancy positions where there's no room to swing the leg behind. Less common than the back flag.

techniques.name: Arm flag
techniques.what: The same counterweight idea, but with a free arm instead of a leg.
techniques.how: Extend the non-holding arm out and away from the wall to shift your mass sideways. Sometimes you just push the wall lightly with the palm.
techniques.best: Slab, delicate balance, and moments where both feet are already committed.

techniques.name: Perching
techniques.what: Standing tall and balanced directly over one high foot, hips stacked above the toe, arms barely loaded.
techniques.how: Get the foot high, shift your hips forward and up over it, then stand up through the leg. Resist pulling with the arms — they're only for balance.
techniques.best: Slab, vertical walls, volumes, and rests. The cheapest way to gain height that exists.

techniques.name: Frogging
techniques.what: Both knees turned out and dropped wide, hips pressed close to the wall.
techniques.how: Turn both feet outward on their inside edges, let the knees splay, and push the pelvis into the wall.
techniques.best: Bringing hips close on vertical and slightly overhanging walls, and for resting. Also a good hip-mobility indicator.

techniques.name: Inside figure 4
techniques.what: You hook a leg over your own arm, on the inside, and sit on it to gain height without footholds.
techniques.how: Hang from one arm, bring the leg on the same side over that forearm, then press down through the leg to push your body up.
techniques.best: Overhangs with no feet — mostly a comp and steep-cave move. High elbow and shoulder load; not a beginner move.

techniques.name: Outside figure 4
techniques.what: Same idea, but the leg hooks over the arm from the outside.
techniques.how: Hang from one arm, swing the opposite leg over that arm from outside, and press up.
techniques.best: Rare, awkward, high-injury-risk. Filed under 'know the name, don't practise it'.

techniques.name: The Janja
techniques.what: Gym slang for the extreme hip-close, deep-turn body position associated with Janja Garnbret's style — usually a very compressed drop-knee-like position where the hips stay glued to the wall through a long move.
techniques.how: Essentially a maximal version of the backstep/drop knee with a lot of hip flexibility and core tension.
techniques.best: Nothing you need yet. The name isn't standardised — check how your gym uses it, because different walls use it for different moves.

techniques.name: Peter Pan
techniques.what: A dynamic move where you launch into a fully extended, briefly airborne position — arms and legs stretched out — before catching the target hold.
techniques.how: Generate from the legs, extend the whole body in flight, and catch the hold at full stretch.
techniques.best: Steep, powerful comp-style problems. Name varies by gym; high impact, so not a beginner priority.

techniques.name: Inside edge
techniques.what: Standing on the big-toe side of the shoe.
techniques.how: Place the front-inside point of the shoe on the hold and drop the heel. Keeps you square to the wall.
techniques.best: Frontal climbing, slab, and any move where you want stability over reach.

techniques.name: Outside edge
techniques.what: Standing on the little-toe side of the shoe.
techniques.how: Roll onto the outer front point and turn the hip in. This is what makes a backstep possible.
techniques.best: Side-on positions, long reaches, and steep walls.

techniques.name: Smear
techniques.what: Using friction against the flat wall or a sloping surface with no defined hold.
techniques.how: Press the ball of the foot flat against the wall, keep the heel low, and push through it. Trust it — hesitation reduces surface contact.
techniques.best: Slab, volumes, and filling gaps where footholds don't exist.

techniques.name: Alpine knee
techniques.what: Putting the knee directly on a hold or ledge instead of the foot.
techniques.how: Kneel onto the hold to gain height, then bring the foot up.
techniques.best: Occasionally the only option outdoors or on a mantle. Frowned upon in the gym, it strips skin, and it puts your kneecap on a hard edge. Learn the rock-over instead.

techniques.name: Heel hook
techniques.what: Placing the heel on a hold and pulling with the hamstring, effectively using the leg as a third arm.
techniques.how: Set the heel on the hold, point the toe slightly outward, then actively pull — think of dragging the hold toward your hips. Keep tension; a loose heel slips.
techniques.best: Steep ground, topping out, and taking weight off the arms. Warm your hamstrings up first — cold heel hooks strain them.

techniques.name: Toe hook
techniques.what: Hooking the top of the foot under or against a hold to stop your body swinging out.
techniques.how: Press the top of the toes against the underside or far side of a hold and pull with the shin and hamstring.
techniques.best: Roofs, steep compression, and stopping a cut-loose from swinging you off.

techniques.name: Bat hang
techniques.what: Hanging upside down from both feet, hands free.
techniques.how: Hook both toes over a solid feature (usually a roof lip or big volume) and let go with the hands.
techniques.best: Roof problems and comp gimmicks. Fun, but a bad fall position — only with pads and supervision.

techniques.name: Bicycle
techniques.what: One foot pushes on a hold while the other toe-hooks the opposite side of the same hold — the two feet squeeze it.
techniques.how: Press with one toe, hook with the other, and clamp. The hold is now held between your feet.
techniques.best: Steep terrain and roofs where you need your feet to stay on while your hands move.

techniques.name: Heel-toe cam
techniques.what: Wedging the foot between two surfaces, heel on one and toe on the other, so the foot locks in place.
techniques.how: Find a slot, corner, or gap between volumes; set the heel on one side and jam the toes against the other until it's snug.
techniques.best: No-hands rests, roofs, and holding position while you shake out. Powerful, and it can trap your ankle — be able to release it.

techniques.name: Frog pinch
techniques.what: Squeezing a volume or large feature between both feet, knees splayed like a frog.
techniques.how: Place both feet on either side of the feature and press inward with the legs.
techniques.best: Comp-style volume climbing. Name varies by gym.

techniques.name: Knee bar
techniques.what: Wedging the leg between two surfaces — knee/thigh pressing one, foot pressing the other — so the leg locks solid.
techniques.how: Slot the foot on one hold, then drive the top of the knee or thigh against the opposing surface until the pressure holds you.
techniques.best: The best rest in climbing when you find one. Often lets you take both hands off. Worth actively hunting for on roofs.

techniques.name: Open hand / three-finger drag
techniques.what: Fingers almost straight, hanging from the last two joints, thumb not involved. Usually index, middle and ring on the hold.
techniques.how: Drape the fingers over the hold and let them extend. It should feel like hanging, not gripping.
techniques.best: The safest and most sustainable grip. Best on slopers, big edges and jugs, and the sensible default for anyone with irritable fingers or elbows.

techniques.name: Open crimp
techniques.what: A slightly closed open hand — fingers curved but the last joint isn't hyperextended.
techniques.how: Curl the fingers gently onto the edge without engaging the thumb.
techniques.best: General-purpose grip on small edges. A good middle ground between drag and half crimp.

techniques.name: Half crimp
techniques.what: Middle knuckles bent to roughly 90 degrees, fingertip joint flat, thumb off.
techniques.how: Set the fingers on the edge, bend the big knuckles to a right angle, and keep the fingertips flat rather than curling.
techniques.best: The most trainable and transferable grip position. This should be your main strength position long-term.

techniques.name: Quarter crimp
techniques.what: Between drag and half crimp — big knuckles bent slightly, fingertip joints still flat.
techniques.how: Half crimp shape with less bend at the knuckle.
techniques.best: Small, positive edges where full half-crimp feels cramped. Common in modern finger training.

techniques.name: Closed crimp / full crimp
techniques.what: Fingertip joints hyperextended and the thumb wrapped over the index finger. 'Closed crimp' and 'full crimp' are used interchangeably by most climbers.
techniques.how: Curl the fingers hard onto a small edge, then lock the thumb over the index fingernail.
techniques.best: Maximum force on tiny edges, and maximum stress on the A2 pulley and the medial elbow. The most common source of pulley injuries — introduce it late, and use it sparingly.

techniques.name: Two-finger pocket
techniques.what: Only two fingers fit the hold.
techniques.how: Usually middle + ring (strongest pairing) or index + middle. Keep the wrist neutral and don't twist.
techniques.best: Pocketed holds. Load builds fast on a small area — introduce gradually.

techniques.name: Front three
techniques.what: Index, middle and ring fingers on the hold; pinky off.
techniques.how: The natural three-finger position for most people.
techniques.best: Medium pockets and edges too small for four fingers.

techniques.name: Back three
techniques.what: Middle, ring and pinky on the hold; index off.
techniques.how: Slide the index off the edge and load the outer three.
techniques.best: Awkward hold orientations and, for some people, a stronger position than front three. Worth testing which of the two is stronger.

techniques.name: Mono
techniques.what: A single finger in a pocket.
techniques.how: Usually the middle finger. Keep the arm aligned under the pocket and avoid any twisting load.
techniques.best: Rare in gyms, brutal on tendons. Not something a beginner should seek out.

techniques.name: Closed mono
techniques.what: A mono with the thumb locked over the finger for extra force.
techniques.how: As above, with the thumb wrapping the finger.
techniques.best: Very high injury risk for very little gain below advanced grades. Know the name; skip the practice.

techniques.name: Stacked fingers
techniques.what: Stacking one finger on top of another in a pocket too small for two side by side.
techniques.how: Place the middle finger in the pocket, then rest the index on top of it to add force.
techniques.best: Small pockets, mostly outdoors. Uncommon in gyms.

techniques.name: Pinch
techniques.what: Squeezing a hold between the fingers and the thumb.
techniques.how: Set the fingers on one side, thumb on the other, and squeeze. Keep the wrist stiff so the force goes into the hold.
techniques.best: Very common in modern setting. Trains thumb strength and is relatively kind to the fingers.

techniques.name: Thumbercling / thumb catch
techniques.what: Using the thumb on the underside or edge of a hold to add direction or stability.
techniques.how: Hook the thumb pad under a lip or against a corner of the hold while the fingers work from above.
techniques.best: Slopers and volumes where the thumb turns a bad hold into a usable one.

techniques.name: Palm down / palming
techniques.what: Pressing with the flat of the palm rather than gripping anything.
techniques.how: Place the palm flat on a volume or the wall and push downward or outward.
techniques.best: Slab, mantles, stemming and rests. Zero finger load, so it is always worth looking for.

techniques.name: Meat hook
techniques.what: Using the fleshy edge of the hand, wrist or forearm hooked over a feature instead of a normal grip.
techniques.how: Drape the side of the hand or forearm over the hold and pull with the arm rather than the fingers.
techniques.best: Big volumes and rounded features. Name varies by gym.

techniques.name: Side pull
techniques.what: A vertically-oriented hold pulled sideways, toward your midline.
techniques.how: Lean your body away from the hold so your weight opposes it, and keep the arm relatively straight.
techniques.best: Extremely common. The key insight: a side pull only works if your body counterbalances it.

techniques.name: Lay back
techniques.what: Pulling on a side pull or edge while pushing with the feet in the opposite direction, body leaning off to the side.
techniques.how: Hands pull one way, feet press the other, and the opposition holds you on. Keep arms straight and walk the feet up.
techniques.best: Aretes, corners, and flakes. Efficient when done with straight arms; exhausting when done with bent ones.

techniques.name: Gaston
techniques.what: A side pull pulled outward, away from your midline, thumb down and elbow out — like prying open a lift door.
techniques.how: Thumb pointing down, elbow high and out, and push/pull outward while your feet push you into the wall.
techniques.best: When the hold faces the wrong way. Shoulder-intensive — keep the elbow from flaring beyond comfort.

techniques.name: Elevator door
techniques.what: Two opposing gastons at the same time — both hands pressing outward, like forcing lift doors apart.
techniques.how: One hand on each hold, elbows out, press outward on both simultaneously and keep body tension.
techniques.best: Symmetrical comp-style sequences. Heavy on the shoulders.

techniques.name: Undercling
techniques.what: A hold gripped from underneath, palm facing up.
techniques.how: Get your feet high so your hips rise above the hold — an undercling only becomes useful once you're above it. Pull up and in.
techniques.best: Under roofs and flakes. High feet are the whole trick.

techniques.name: Compression
techniques.what: Squeezing two opposing holds or features toward each other to stay on.
techniques.how: Hands (and often feet) press inward from both sides. Body tension holds the whole thing together.
techniques.best: Volumes, aretes and prows. Very common in modern setting.

techniques.name: Inverted
techniques.what: Any position where your hips are above your shoulders — upside down or nearly so.
techniques.how: Usually reached via a toe hook or bat hang, with heavy core engagement.
techniques.best: Roofs. Disorienting, so learn it low with pads.

techniques.name: Outward facing
techniques.what: Climbing with your back or side to the wall rather than your chest.
techniques.how: Turn out and use the wall behind you for pressure, often with a heel hook or stem.
techniques.best: Corners, chimneys, and awkward comp volumes.

techniques.name: Gastondercling
techniques.what: A hybrid where a hold is used as a gaston and an undercling at once — elbow out, palm rotated up.
techniques.how: Thumb-down gaston grip while the pull direction is upward from underneath.
techniques.best: Awkward hold orientations. Slang, and not universal.

techniques.name: Lock off
techniques.what: Holding a static bent-arm position so the other hand can reach.
techniques.how: Pull the hold to chest or shoulder height, engage the shoulder, and hold still while the other arm moves.
techniques.best: Precise reaches to bad holds. Note: this is the single most elbow-loading position in climbing — prefer deadpointing when elbows are irritable.

techniques.name: Stemming / bridging
techniques.what: Pressing outward with both feet (and sometimes hands) against two opposing surfaces.
techniques.how: Feet wide on either side of a corner or between two volumes, push outward, and stand tall.
techniques.best: Corners and dihedrals. Often a full no-hands rest — worth spotting.

techniques.name: The chin
techniques.what: Using the chin, head or shoulder to press against a hold or volume for a moment of extra stability.
techniques.how: Press the chin or side of the head onto the hold while both hands reposition.
techniques.best: Almost entirely a comp trick. Real, occasionally decisive, and mildly ridiculous.

techniques.name: Hand match
techniques.what: Both hands on the same hold.
techniques.how: Make room by shifting the first hand to one side, then bring the second alongside. On small holds, move fingers one at a time.
techniques.best: Changing lead hand. Fundamental.

techniques.name: Piano match
techniques.what: Matching by walking the fingers across a hold one at a time, like piano keys.
techniques.how: Lift and replace individual fingers of the first hand while the second hand's fingers take their place.
techniques.best: Small edges where there's no room for a normal match.

techniques.name: Foot match
techniques.what: Both feet on the same hold, or swapping which foot is on it.
techniques.how: Either share the hold, or hop-swap: quick, quiet, controlled. Keep hands on and hips close during the swap.
techniques.best: Changing which side of your body leads. Extremely common.

techniques.name: Hand-foot match
techniques.what: A hand and a foot on the same hold at the same time.
techniques.how: Grip the hold, then bring the toe onto the same hold beside your fingers — usually to the outside of the hand.
techniques.best: Roofs, mantles, and steep problems with sparse feet. Watch your fingers.

techniques.name: Hand cross (over)
techniques.what: Reaching one hand over the other to a hold on the far side.
techniques.how: Turn the hips side-on first, then cross the arm over the top. Crossing without turning the hips is what makes it feel impossible.
techniques.best: Traverses and diagonal sequences. Saves an intermediate move.

techniques.name: Hand cross (under)
techniques.what: Crossing one arm underneath the other.
techniques.how: Drop the shoulder and pass the arm below. Often more stable than crossing over.
techniques.best: Undercling sequences and low traverses.

techniques.name: Rose move
techniques.what: A dramatic cross where the reaching arm passes behind your own head to a hold on the far side.
techniques.how: Turn fully side-on, drop the shoulder, and reach back and across, usually to a gaston or side pull.
techniques.best: Rare, showy, and genuinely useful on some diagonal sequences. Shoulder-intensive.

techniques.name: Foot cross (front)
techniques.what: Crossing one foot in front of the other to reach a hold on the far side.
techniques.how: Keep hips close, cross the free foot in front, and place precisely without bumping the standing leg.
techniques.best: Traverses. Often better than a series of small foot shuffles.

techniques.name: Foot cross (back)
techniques.what: Crossing one foot behind the other.
techniques.how: Sweep the foot behind the standing leg and place it. Naturally turns you side-on.
techniques.best: Traverses where crossing in front would push your hips off the wall.

techniques.name: Rock over
techniques.what: Shifting your centre of gravity from below a high foot to above it, then standing up on it.
techniques.how: Get the foot high, push your hips forward and over the toe, keep the shoulders coming with you, then press through the leg.
techniques.best: Slab and vertical walls. This is the move that converts leg strength into height, and a high priority for any beginner.

techniques.name: Knee press
techniques.what: Pressing the knee or shin into the wall or a volume for stability.
techniques.how: Drive the knee into the surface to create friction and stop rotation while a hand moves.
techniques.best: Volumes and slab. A cheap stabiliser.

techniques.name: Mantle
techniques.what: Pushing down on a hold or ledge to get your body above it, like climbing out of a swimming pool.
techniques.how: Pull to chest height, rotate the hand so the palm presses down, press until the arm locks, then bring a foot up.
techniques.best: Topping out. Essential and often the crux of a problem for beginners.

techniques.name: Beached whale
techniques.what: The inelegant version of a mantle — flopping the torso onto the ledge and wriggling up.
techniques.how: Belly on the ledge, then squirm.
techniques.best: Getting up when the clean mantle fails. It counts. It just doesn't look good.

techniques.name: Cut loose
techniques.what: Letting both feet come off the wall so your body swings, then re-engaging them.
techniques.how: Accept the swing, keep the core tight, control the return, and put the feet back deliberately rather than scrabbling.
techniques.best: Steep ground where feet can't follow the hands. Often faster than fighting to keep them on.

techniques.name: Campussing
techniques.what: Climbing with no feet at all, hand over hand.
techniques.how: Pull between holds using arms only.
techniques.best: Sometimes the intended sequence on steep problems. Very high elbow and shoulder load, and a leading cause of climber's elbow — avoid until well adapted.

techniques.name: The Houdini
techniques.what: Escaping a tangled or reversed body position by rotating through it rather than reversing the moves.
techniques.how: Usually a hip rotation under an arm to unwind crossed limbs.
techniques.best: Getting out of a sequence you read wrong. Name varies by gym.

techniques.name: Good Samaritan
techniques.what: Using a hold or feature that isn't part of your problem — or one hand helping the other — to save a position.
techniques.how: Grab whatever is available to stabilise, usually mid-fall or mid-mistake.
techniques.best: Practically: a bail-out. Off-route holds mean the send doesn't count. Name varies by gym.

techniques.name: T-Rex turtle roll
techniques.what: Gym slang for rolling the body over a lip or volume with arms tucked close, when there's nothing to push on.
techniques.how: Commit the hips over the feature and roll, keeping the arms in tight.
techniques.best: Awkward topouts on rounded features. Definitely slang — expect your gym to have its own name.

techniques.name: Dead point
techniques.what: Catching the hold at the weightless instant at the top of an upward move.
techniques.how: Generate from the legs, and time the hand to arrive exactly when your upward momentum stops. Not before, not after.
techniques.best: Almost every reach. Cheaper than a lock-off and far kinder to the elbows. The most important item in this section.

techniques.name: Dyno
techniques.what: A jump where all four points leave the wall.
techniques.how: Load the legs by dropping into a coil, drive upward through the feet, and keep your eyes on the target hold the whole time.
techniques.best: Moves that are simply too far to reach. Fun, high-impact — a couple per session, not a training focus.

techniques.name: Double dyno
techniques.what: A dyno caught with both hands simultaneously.
techniques.how: As above, but keep the body square so both hands arrive together.
techniques.best: Big jugs and comp-style jumps. Landing one is a power indicator, not a reason to build a session around them.

techniques.name: One-arm dyno
techniques.what: A dyno caught on a single hand.
techniques.how: Generate from the legs and lead with the catching arm; the other arm stays back for balance.
techniques.best: Comp problems. Very high shoulder and elbow impact.

techniques.name: Double clutch
techniques.what: A dyno where both hands leave, one hand catches briefly, and the other immediately follows or bumps onward.
techniques.how: Catch and stabilise with the first hand while the second arrives in the same motion.
techniques.best: Steep sequences with no intermediate holds. Advanced.

techniques.name: Paddle dyno (triple / quadruple)
techniques.what: A dyno where a hand slaps one or more intermediate holds mid-flight to redirect momentum before the real catch.
techniques.how: Use each intermediate slap to push or steer rather than to hold.
techniques.best: Comp setting. Spectacular, rarely necessary.

techniques.name: Step-up dyno
techniques.what: A dyno generated by stepping up onto a high foot and springing from it, rather than coiling both legs.
techniques.how: Place the high foot, load it, and drive upward through that single leg.
techniques.best: When the feet are too high or awkward for a two-legged coil.

techniques.name: Hip swing
techniques.what: Generating momentum by swinging the hips rather than pulling with the arms.
techniques.how: Initiate the swing from the core and time the hand release to the peak.
techniques.best: Steep ground. This is how strong climbers make hard moves look easy.

techniques.name: Arm swing
techniques.what: Using the free arm's swing to add momentum to a move.
techniques.how: Swing the free arm upward in time with the leg drive.
techniques.best: Adds a surprising amount to a dyno or long reach.

techniques.name: Pogo / moon kick
techniques.what: Kicking one leg out and down to generate momentum, like a pogo stick, when there are no useful footholds.
techniques.how: Swing the free leg down and back hard, and use the reaction to drive your body up toward the hold.
techniques.best: Steep problems with one foothold and a long move. Looks strange, works well.

techniques.name: Run and jump
techniques.what: A dyno started from the ground with running steps.
techniques.how: Two or three steps into the wall, then jump for the start or first hold.
techniques.best: Comp-style jump starts. Uncontrolled landings — pads and spotters.

techniques.name: Swing and jump
techniques.what: Building a pendulum swing on the holds, then releasing at the peak into a jump.
techniques.how: Swing the body once or twice to build amplitude, release at the top of the arc.
techniques.best: Roofs and comp problems where a static jump can't reach.

techniques.name: Headbutt
techniques.what: Using the head or forehead pressed against a volume for a moment of stability, usually during compression.
techniques.how: Press the head into the surface to add a third contact point while hands reposition.
techniques.best: Rare comp trick. Real, but not something to seek out.

drillSection.title: Drill Bank
drillSection.intro: Constraints make an easy problem hard without adding load to fingers and elbows. Pick **one** per session and apply it to V1–V3. Rotate so you're not always training the same weakness.

drillCategories.title: Movement drills
callouts: On grip work: bias heavily toward open hand and half crimp. Full crimping is the highest-stress grip for both fingers and elbow, and it is the last thing a beginner needs to train.

drillCategories.title: Volume & fun games
callouts: Circuits and traverses are pump-heavy. On a day when something already aches, choose a precision drill instead of a volume game.

drills.name: Silent feet
drills.description: climb an easy problem with zero foot noise. Any scrape or slap, repeat the move.

drills.name: Glue feet
drills.description: once a foot is placed it cannot move again until it leaves for the next hold. No shuffling.

drills.name: Sniper
drills.description: chalk a small dot on each foothold; the toe must land on the dot.

drills.name: Outside edge only
drills.description: every foot placement uses the little-toe edge. Forces backsteps and hip turns.

drills.name: Feet eliminated
drills.description: remove the two best footholds from the problem. Same holds for hands, new puzzle.

drills.name: Smear only
drills.description: on slab or vertical, no footholds at all; only the wall surface.

drills.name: Foot swap
drills.description: every foothold must be used by both feet at some point, swapped without moving your hands.

drills.name: Big-foot
drills.description: you may only use volumes and the biggest holds for feet. Forces long, committing steps.

drills.name: Toe drag
drills.description: keep the trailing toe in contact with the wall through every move. Kills the dangling leg habit.

drills.name: Straight arms only
drills.description: if an elbow bends, you're off the problem. Forces backsteps and flags.

drills.name: Hip kiss
drills.description: the hip must touch or nearly touch the wall on every move.

drills.name: Flag hunt
drills.description: every move must include a flag of some kind. Ridiculous on some problems, which is the point.

drills.name: Backstep everything
drills.description: use a backstep on every move that physically allows one.

drills.name: No barn-door
drills.description: if your body swings open at any point, restart. Teaches you to feel it coming.

drills.name: One-arm sections
drills.description: on easy jugs, remove one hand entirely for 2–3 moves and move with legs only.

drills.name: One foot only
drills.description: climb an easy problem using a single foot; the other leg never touches a hold and works purely as a counterweight.

drills.name: Slow motion
drills.description: 10 seconds per move. You can't hide bad balance behind momentum.

drills.name: Hover
drills.description: hold the hand 5 cm from the target hold for 3 seconds before grabbing.

drills.name: One-touch
drills.description: the hand lands on a hold and stays. No readjusting, no bumping.

drills.name: Continuous flow
drills.description: no pause at all, metronome rhythm, top to bottom. The opposite of slow motion; train both.

drills.name: Static then dynamic
drills.description: climb the same problem twice, once as statically as possible, once as dynamically as possible.

drills.name: Downclimb everything
drills.description: climb up, then reverse it to the ground. Free footwork practice and it doubles your volume.

drills.name: Deadpoint practice
drills.description: on an easy problem, make every hand move a small controlled pop rather than a reach.

drills.name: Quiet hands
drills.description: no slapping, no re-gripping, no chalking mid-problem.

drills.name: Grip awareness
drills.description: climb an easy problem consciously choosing a grip for each hold: open hand, half crimp, pinch, sloper. The goal is deliberate choice, not maximum grip.

drills.name: Predict and verify
drills.description: write or say the full sequence out loud before pulling on, then check it against what actually happened.

drills.name: Onsight only
drills.description: for one session, every problem gets exactly one attempt. Forces real reading.

drills.name: Blind feet
drills.description: read the problem, then climb without looking down at your feet.

drills.name: Reverse read
drills.description: read the problem from the top down before climbing it bottom-up.

drills.name: Two solutions
drills.description: find and climb two genuinely different sequences for the same problem.

drills.name: Add-on
drills.description: you do move 1, partner adds move 2, alternate until someone falls.

drills.name: Take-away
drills.description: alternate removing one hold from a problem until it becomes unclimbable. Last person to send wins.

drills.name: Caller
drills.description: partner calls each hold out loud while you climb. You may only use what's called.

drills.name: Mirror
drills.description: partner climbs a problem; you repeat it move for move, exactly, including foot placements.

drills.name: Technique referee
drills.description: partner watches and counts errors: foot readjustments, bent arms, noisy feet. Lowest score wins.

drills.name: Dice / roulette
drills.description: assign a constraint to each number, roll before each problem.

drills.name: Traverse the wall
drills.description: link the start holds of every problem across a section.

drills.name: Colour chaos
drills.description: pick one hold colour and climb anywhere on the wall using only that colour.

drills.name: Ladder
drills.description: V1 → V2 → V3 → V2 → V1 back to back, then rest 5 minutes.

drills.name: Circuit of four
drills.description: four V1–V2 problems in a row with no rest, then 3 minutes off. Repeat 3–4 times.

drills.name: Pyramid session
drills.description: 4 problems at V1, 3 at V2, 2 at V3, 1 project. A complete session in itself.

drills.name: Speed–quality
drills.description: climb a V1 as fast as possible, then as perfectly as possible. Compare how it felt.

drills.name: No-repeat hour
drills.description: every problem you climb in the session must be one you've never done before.
